articles.title: ‘Ghetto’: Laura Loomer must be denounced for racist comments
articles.summary: If Republicans cannot simply say that racism is wrong, that 9/11 is not an inside job, and that President Trump should disassociate himself from people who traffic in this kind of hateful, vile and bigoted rhetoric, then what are we even talking about?
articles.body:
Laura Loomer is racist and obviously very obsessed with Black women.

If you missed what this uncivilized clown had to say — and no, I’m not calling Loomer a clown because people online compare her to Jigsaw from “Saw.” I’m calling her a clown because her behavior is clownish — she went after Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, Reps. Ilhan Omar and Ayanna Pressley, former Rep. Cori Bush and Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, calling them “ghetto, entitled, race-obsessed, destructive Black b*****s” and saying they were unfit for the power they hold.

The least funny part about all of this is the silence from the Republican Party.

Former Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene actually condemned Loomer, calling her comments “nasty, hateful” and racist. Greene went even further, saying, “This is Trump’s new MAGA and Republican Party and I want nothing to do with it.”

So where are the rest of the Republicans who claim racism has no place in American society?

Because I keep hearing from them about Hasan Piker. And if Piker is politically relevant enough to generate scrutiny because he has campaigned with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, then surely Loomer, an unofficial Trump adviser, who has campaigned with Donald Trump, has his cellphone number, has met with him in the Oval Office, has been welcomed inside the White House, and touts moving the needle on policy decisions, is relevant enough to warrant the same scrutiny.

“Your president refuses to condemn this. That is the overarching point, I do not want to hear a single thing about Hasan Piker until your president goes forward and condemns this.”

Because this isn’t about whether Hasan Piker or Laura Loomer is more offensive. It’s about whether the standard actually exists or not.

Let’s not pretend Loomer is some random woman yelling into the internet. Trump has publicly praised her work, and reporting has documented her access to him and her influence inside his political orbit. In April 2025, she met with Trump in the Oval Office and pushed him to oust personnel she believed were disloyal.

This is the same woman who promoted conspiracy theories about 9/11 , yet Trump brought her to a 9/11 memorial event during the 2024 campaign.

So when Republicans demand accountability for inflammatory rhetoric from people associated with Democrats, I agree with them. Accountability cannot be partisan.

But if you want to pretend that Loomer has no connection to Trump, there are a slew of other statements made by Republican government officials that Republicans can condemn. Our colleague Niall Stanage summed it up seamlessly :

“The president of the United States described people of Somalia as garbage. Randy Fine, a Republican congressman, compared muslims unfavorably to dogs. The Republican nominee for Senate in Georgia tweeted a video at the time of pro-Palestine protests of a white counter-protester racially abusing a Black woman. Those are not influencers, those are the president of the United States and office holders in this time.”

I’m disgusted that we have reached a place where calling out racism somehow requires a political calculation. Black women should not have to be perfect to deserve basic human dignity. And political parties should not need a polling memo before deciding that racism is wrong.

If Republicans cannot simply say that racism is wrong, that 9/11 is not an inside job, and that President Trump should disassociate himself from people who traffic in this kind of hateful, vile and bigoted rhetoric, then what are we even talking about? Silence is permission. The Republican Party is going to need to find the backbone to condemn hate when it comes from people inside its own orbit.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

Oyer was dismissed in March 2025, one of many in an early wave of dismissals and reassignments at the DOJ in the…
articles.body:
Former U.S. pardon attorney Liz Oyer is suing the Department of Justice (DOJ) over her termination, which took place last year after she refused to recommend that actor Mel Gibson have his gun rights restored.

Oyer was dismissed in March 2025, one of many in an early wave of dismissals and reassignments at the DOJ in the first few months of the Trump administration.

“Shortly after President Trump took office, Ms. Oyer was asked to disregard her duties and facilitate a political favor for the actor Mel Gibson, based on Mr. Gibson’s relationship with President Trump. Ms. Oyer was asked to make it seem like an independent review had concluded that Mr. Gibson, who was convicted of a domestic violence offense, should have his gun rights restored,” states the suit , which was filed on Oyer’s behalf through the nonprofit Democracy Forward.

“Ms. Oyer had serious concerns about the public safety implications of granting Mr. Gibson’s request in light of his history of domestic violence and the well-documented dangers of placing firearms in the hands of domestic abusers.” Like others fired under the Trump administration, Oyer received a short termination notice saying she was being fired under the president’s authority as granted by Article 2 of the Constitution, the article that establishes the presidency.

That process failed to follow various protections afforded to civil servants, including 30 days’ notice and the opportunity to respond in writing and receive “a written decision specifying the reasons for the removal.”

“This case is about much more than what happened to me. All Americans rely on nonpartisan civil servants to keep them safe and to uphold the law without fear or favor. I was fired because I refused to put politics ahead of my duty to the American people. My firing violated my constitutional and statutory rights, and it also jeopardized public safety,” Oyer said in a statement.

“That is not how the Department of Justice is supposed to operate, and it is not how public servants in this country should be treated. If career officials like me can be fired for refusing to bend the rules to serve the president’s friends, then the message to every public servant is clear: loyalty to a politician matters more than loyalty to the Constitution. I cannot accept that.”

The suit also argues that her termination violated her First Amendment rights because the removal was based on Oyer’s perceived political affiliation given her hiring under the Biden administration.

After filing Oyer, Trump installed Ed Martin as the pardon attorney . Martin, a conservative activist who represented a number of Jan. 6 rioters, had previously been nominated to serve as a U.S. attorney but failed to advance in the Senate over concerns about his work on behalf of such clients.

The suit says Oyer is bringing her claims to court after an earlier filing before the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) effectively stalled.

“The MSPB has proved, however, to be a dead end. Despite filing her MSPB appeal more than sixteen months ago, she has yet to receive any substantive review of her termination,” Thursday’s court filing states, adding that her case was recently punted again, “sending her case to a further prolonged limbo.”

“In March 2026, the MSPB also issued a decision broadly holding that it lacks jurisdiction in many cases in which the appellant employee was removed in a purported exercise of Article II authority, rather than” through the Civil Service Reform Act.

articles.title: Billionaire Leon Black sues House Oversight Committee over Epstein probe subpoenas
articles.summary: Leon Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor, sued the House Oversight Committee, seeking to stop the panel from enforcing its subpoenas against him in an ongoing Epstein probe.
articles.body: Leon Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor, on Thursday sued the House Oversight Committee, seeking to stop the panel from enforcing its subpoenas against him in an ongoing probe of the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. “The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power,” Black’s attorney, Susan Estrich, said in a statement. Black had been set to appear before the committee Thursday morning. The lawsuit comes after Black voluntarily sat for a closed-door transcribed interview with the Oversight Committee in late June but left the hearing early. Lawmakers have for months sought more information on the financial web that allowed Epstein to fund his sex trafficking operation and whether Black was at all involved or aware of any illegal activity. They specifically have sought information about any nondisclosure agreements Black signed with women. Black has denied any wrongdoing, involvement in or awareness of Epstein’s illegal activity. In Thursday’s statement, she said that Black was “misled” about the intentions of the committee’s chair, Rep. James Comer, R-Ky. “Mr. Black has cooperated with the Committee by voluntarily appearing to answer questions in a transcribed interview. Despite being misled about the intent of that interview, he then fully complied with the Committee’s subpoena related to Epstein,” Estrich said. She added, “To imply misconduct because of the existence of a confidentiality agreement is entirely unjustified. Confidentiality agreements are routinely used in business.” Estrich went on to wholly deny any allegations against Black, saying, “We want to reiterate that Mr. Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein’s arrest in 2019. Mr. Black never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein.” Black’s name appears more than 300 times in files released by the Justice Department late last year and early this year related to Epstein. His name appears often in emails from Epstein’s assistant, directing the financier to call Black. More than 100 of the mentions of Black are in emails from Epstein’s assistant, who wrote, “Leon Black returned your call.” In a statement, Comer reacted to Black’s failure to appear before the committee Thursday, saying, “It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people.” He added, “Mr. Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation as he was one of Mr. Epstein’s fee paying clients and has several non-disclosure agreements. Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr. Black. I will speak with our members about next steps.” Black’s career and his reputation have been marred for years due to his relationship with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender who died in 2019. In 2022, Black was sued over allegations that he raped a woman in Epstein’s New York City mansion in 2002. That case was later dropped with prejudice after both parties reached an agreement to do so and Black denied the allegations against him. A separate but ongoing lawsuit, filed in 2023, accused Black of raping a 16-year-old girl at Epstein’s Manhattan townhouse in 2002. A lawyer for Black denied the allegations, calling them “frivolous and sanctionable.” In April, a judge overseeing the case wrote that the plaintiff and her attorney “engaged in serious, sanctionable misconduct in this case,” but allowed the case to proceed. Black in 2021 stepped down from the hedge fund he co-founded, Apollo Global Management, after the firm conducted an independent review looking into his ties to Epstein. The review found that Black was not involved in Epstein’s criminal activities. Earlier this year, he was set to be deposed in a lawsuit filed by survivors of Epstein and his associates alleging that Bank of America facilitated and profited from Epstein’s illegal sex trafficking activity. Bank of America later settled that lawsuit for more than $70 million and did not admit any liability in that case. “While we stand by our prior statements made in the filings in this case, including that Bank of America did not facilitate sex trafficking crimes, this resolution allows us to put this matter behind us and provides further closure for the plaintiffs,” a Bank of America spokesperson told NBC News at the time. In a statement reacting to news of the lawsuit Thursday, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said, “By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two Congressional subpoenas. Black gave Jeffrey Epstein over $180 million over six years. He funded Epstein’s abuse and trafficking of women. Multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable.” Garcia also called to hold Black in contempt of Congress.

articles.title: Could Lindsay Clancy walk free after a mistrial?
articles.summary: Legal experts say other options include offering Clancy a plea deal or deciding not to put her on trial again.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A Massachusetts jury is deliberating Thursday for a sixth day on whether Lindsay Clancy is criminally responsible for the strangling deaths of her three children in 2023, amid conflicting testimony about her post-pregnancy mental health.

For a second time, jurors on Wednesday told the judge they were still unable to reach a unanimous verdict . They were sent back to try again with a Tuey-Rodriguez charge instruction. Also known as a “ dynamite charge ,” the instruction is used when a jury is deadlocked.

So, what happens if jurors can’t reach a verdict?

Massachusetts requires a unanimous verdict. If jurors can’t agree, the judge would push them to keep deliberating. If they remain deadlocked , the result is a mistrial, and prosecutors would be free to retry the case before a new jury.

If a mistrial is declared, the case would essentially go back to the same status as before the trial, with the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse charged with murder and held at a psychiatric hospital awaiting a resolution of the criminal case.

Prosecutors would have to decide whether to try again with a new jury. If they do, the jury selection process would begin again and a new trial would be scheduled.

Prosecutors could also offer Clancy a plea deal, Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and former prosecutor who is not involved in the case, told the Associated Press .

“Any time the threat of a retrial with murder one hanging over the client is re-interjected, defense lawyers will, at the very least, explore whether or not there’s any interest in a resolution,” Bailey said.

Clancy’s defense contends she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and should not be found guilty.

After the killings, her husband found her badly injured in the yard, where she landed after jumping from a second-story window. She was left paralyzed from the waist down .

Prosecutors argued she understood what she was doing and should be held criminally responsible.

Though less likely after a first trial ends without a verdict, the district attorney’s office could decide to not retry the case.

What possible verdicts could Clancy face?

If jurors find Clancy criminally responsible and convict her of first-degree murder, she would face a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

A second-degree murder conviction also carries a life sentence but with eventual parole eligibility.

Under Massachusetts law, the burden is entirely on prosecutors to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when she killed her children.

To do that, they must show either that she wasn’t suffering from a mental disease or defect or that she was still able to understand her actions were wrong and control herself despite it.

Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, has argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and lacked criminal responsibility.

His final witness, forensic psychiatrist Dr. Phillip Resnick — who also testified for Andrea Yates’ defense in 2006 — told jurors Clancy was “clearly psychotic” the day of the killings and believed, delusionally, that her children would be better off dying with her than being taken by social services.

A not-guilty finding on these grounds would not mean Clancy goes free.

The judge allowed for the possibility of a manslaughter verdict before the case was handed over to the jury.

NewsNation’s Damita Menezes, Laura Ingle and Safia Samee Ali, and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Vance says he won’t turn on ‘friend’ Carlson over Trump, Rogers criticism
articles.summary: Vice President Vance defended his relationship with right-wing media personality Tucker Carlson during Thursday’s White House press briefing, saying he won’t allow political disagreements to ruin friendships. Carlson this past week has said President Trump should be removed from office for “actively considering” preemptive nuclear strikes, while also saying he wouldn’t vote for former Rep.…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance defended his relationship with right-wing media personality Tucker Carlson during Thursday’s White House press briefing, saying he won’t allow political disagreements to ruin friendships.

Carlson this past week has said President Trump should be removed from office for “actively considering” preemptive nuclear strikes, while also saying he wouldn’t vote for former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the GOP candidate in Michigan’s Senate race, “at gunpoint.”

“Everybody knows that Tucker Carlson and I are friends, and I think it’s very obvious that Tucker has said some things that I disagree with,” Vance said when asked Thursday about people who are uneasy about his relationship with the former Fox News host.

“He said some things about the president of the United States that I think are just wrong,” he added.

The vice president also said he disagreed with Carlson’s apparent support of Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers’s Democratic opponent in the Wolverine State.

“I’d like to have a non-crazy person like Mike Rogers representing Michigan in the United States Senate, rather than a crazy person like El-Sayed,” Vance said during the White House press briefing.

However, he went on to say that he tries not to let political disagreements define his friendships.

“Tucker is a friend of mine,” the vice president continued. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things. And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them.”

“I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go,” he added.

Carlson described El-Sayed’s campaign as “Trumpian” during a podcast episode released Wednesday.

The right-wing pundit has long been a major booster of Trump but has been increasingly critical of him since the Iran war started early this year. Both Carlson and Vance have promoted an isolationist, anti-war worldview distinct from more traditional Republican hawkishness.

While Vance has not been publicly critical of the war, he has reportedly been the most skeptical member of Trump’s Cabinet throughout the conflict.

Carlson pointed to the president’s threat of the “total destruction” of Iran in his comments calling for his removal.

“The second any president actively considers first-use of nuclear weapons, that person should be removed from office immediately. Immediately, because that’s gotta be the red line, destroying all of humanity with a nuclear strike,” Carlson said.

“Why isn’t there an attempt to remove him from office, like, immediately?” he added.

articles.title: Advocates decry US House vote to defund universities that boycott Israel
articles.summary: Rights groups say the measure infringes on the freedom of speech of Americans for the benefit of a foreign nation.
articles.body:
The United States House of Representatives has passed a bill to penalise American universities for boycotting Israel or its academic institutions, including those located in the occupied West Bank , a move that critics say violates freedom of expression.

Lawmakers approved the measure in a 237-169 vote on Thursday, with 33 Democrats joining the Republican majority. Two Republicans broke ranks with their party to reject the bill.

The proposal will still needs to be adopted by the Republican-controlled Senate and signed by President Donald Trump to become law.

If passed, it would bar universities that boycott “an entity licensed or regulated by, or organised under the laws of” Israel, such as those in illegal West Bank settlements, from receiving federal funds.

Withholding such funding would make it nearly impossible for many universities to operate or provide financial aid to students.

Jenin Younes, president of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), said the bill raises serious concerns for the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects freedom of speech rights.

“The Supreme Court has made clear that the government cannot condition its funding on suppression of First Amendment-protected activity,” Younes told Al Jazeera. “Courts also recognise that boycotts constitute such activity.”

The legislation would require academic institutions in the US to annually certify that they allow cooperation with Israeli universities. The stipulation raises concerns that the bill not only bans boycotts of schools in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank but could compel US universities to forge relationships with them to fulfil the certification requirement.

The International Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Israeli settlements in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, “have been established and are being maintained in violation of international law”.

The bill comes at a time when public support for Israel in the US has nosedived . A Pew Research Center survey in July suggested that 62 percent of Americans have an unfavourable view of the Israeli government.

Still, support for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which carried out the genocidal war on Gaza, remains strong on Capitol Hill.

“The timing of the bill reflects the Israel lobby’s growing desperation in the face of rising opposition to US support for Israel,” Younes said.

“As Americans’ sentiment turns against our unholy alliance, Israel and its servants in Congress are working overtime to come up with ways to silence dissent and keep Americans’ tax dollars flowing to the genocidal, apartheid state.”

She added that including Israeli colleges in the occupied West Bank in the anti-boycott bill is further evidence there is no real intent by the US “to hold Israel accountable for its unlawful occupation or to pave the way for a Palestinian state”.

For years, US states and Congress have been passing bills to restrict the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement that aims to pressure Israel economically to end abuses against Palestinians.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has been among rights groups who have regularly warned that anti-BDS laws violate constitutional free speech guarantees.

Robert McCaw, CAIR’s government affairs director, called the legislative proposal “a blatant attempt to hold American students’ financial futures hostage in order to shield the Israeli government and entities operating under Israeli law from peaceful economic pressure”.

“Students and faculty have the right to speak, organise and urge their institutions to align investment and purchasing decisions with their values,” McCaw said in a statement.

“Congress should not threaten Pell Grants and student loans simply because lawmakers dislike the outcome of that advocacy,” he said, referring to a federally funded financial aid programme.

Supporters of the bill have argued that the measure aims to regulate commercial conduct, not speech.

“Our universities should not use taxpayer-funded federal programs to discriminate against Israeli students, faculty, institutions, or businesses simply because they are Israeli,” Representative Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House Committee on Education and Workforce, said in a statement.

“I’m proud of my colleagues for standing up for that principle today and I hope to see the Senate do the same,” he said.

Some rights advocates have called for academic boycotts of Israel, saying Israeli universities play a role in enabling abuses against Palestinians by developing weapon systems and military strategies.

“For decades, Israeli universities have played a key role in planning, implementing and justifying Israel’s occupation and apartheid policies, and now genocide, while maintaining a uniquely close relationship with the Israeli military,” the BDS movement website says.

The two Republicans who voted against the bill on Tuesday were Thomas Massie and Warren Davidson, who have both been critical of Washington’s policy towards the Middle East.

The 33 Democrats who approved the measure included staunchly pro-Israel legislators Ritchie Torres and Haley Stevens, who recently lost her bid for the US Senate Democratic Party nomination in Michigan to Abdul El-Sayed , a supporter of Palestinian rights.

articles.title: ‘I wouldn’t call it a war,’ Vance says after Iran hostilities flare
articles.summary: Vice President Vance said Thursday that he wouldn’t call the military operation between the U.S. and Iran “a war,” despite the eruption of hostilities this week. “I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting. I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” he said during the press…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance said Thursday that he wouldn’t call the military operation between the U.S. and Iran “a war,” despite the eruption of hostilities this week.

“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting. I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” he said during the press briefing.

The back-and-forth military strikes this week marked the largest outbreak of fighting in weeks, following a month of relative calm. On Tuesday, the U.S. military carried out roughly 100 strikes against Iranian targets for what it described as retaliation for threats in the Strait of Hormuz.

Vance said it was ultimately up to Iran as to when the fighting would end completely.

“You’re asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?” he said. “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”

He said the U.S. would not rely “on the Iranians behaving responsibly or negotiating in good faith, what we’re going to do is use the tools that we have at our disposal to ensure that the American people, one, never have to deal with the threat of an Iranian nuclear program, and two, that world energy markets are properly supplied.”

The vice president also said he was “extremely skeptical” of reports from Iranian officials that a U.S. missile strike killed at least four civilians at a home in southern Iran where people were celebrating a wedding.

“I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this,” Vance said. “What I can say with 100 percent confidence is that, unlike the IRGC [Iran Revolutionary Guard Corps], the United States never targets civilians in combat.”

He said he had been briefed on the incident and an investigation into it was ongoing.

“We never will do that,” he said of specifically targeting civilians. “We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen, but in this particular case, I don’t think that we have any information one way or the other.”

Vance also addressed an NBC News report that cyberattacks from Iran have targeted U.S. infrastructure.

“What I would say is that we feel quite confident the homeland is safe,” Vance said. “We also feel quite confident that the Iranians are going to try to do a lot of things that they don’t have the capability to do, and that the American people should know that your government is obsessively focused on both anticipating any potential cyber threats but also responding to them appropriately and ensuring they don’t happen.”

He said he would be “much more worried about cyberattacks from other actors.”

NBC News reported Wednesday that Iranian hackers have targeted U.S. water systems, telecommunications, energy and other infrastructure.

The attempted attacks have not been successful, sources told the outlet, and have focused on automated systems connected to the internet.

articles.title: Merz keeps distance on campaign trail ahead of key eastern German vote
articles.summary: During his second campaign visit to Saxony-Anhalt, Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again warned of the economic and social consequences of a potential state g...
articles.body:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz warns against voting for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Saxony-Anhalt state government elections, emphasizing the importance of keeping Germany open and liberal.

Merz's campaign visits in Saxony-Anhalt have lacked direct contact with voters, with meetings limited to management, works council, and state officials, as he criticizes the AfD's stance on the European Union.

The AfD, ahead in the polls for the upcoming state parliament elections, has not explicitly called for withdrawal from the EU, despite Merz's concerns about the party's anti-EU sentiments.

During his second campaign visit to Saxony-Anhalt, Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again warned of the economic and social consequences of a potential state government run by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"Anyone who wants Germany to remain an open and liberal country, and anyone who wants Saxony-Anhalt to remain an attractive location - including from a European perspective - must not vote for the AfD on Sunday," Merz said in the town of Leuna on Thursday during a joint visit to the UPM biorefinery with state Premier Sven Schulze.

As with Merz's first campaign appearance in Quedlinburg, there was no direct contact with voters - apart from a few refinery staff. Merz, who leads the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), met only the management and the works council.

State parliament elections are due to be held in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. In the polls, the AfD is well ahead and stands a chance of securing an absolute majority.

Merz made his first appearance on the campaign trail on Monday, just under a week before the election. Together with Schulze, he visited the latter's birthplace, Quedlinburg in the Harz Mountains, and met members of the state parliament and local officials.

There was no direct contact with voters there either. As in Leuna, only a joint statement in front of the cameras was planned, with no questions from the journalists present.

Merz criticizes the AfD's stance on the EU

In Leuna, Merz criticized in particular the AfD's stance on the European Union. "Anyone who, like the AfD, wants to leave the single market, leave Schengen and leave the European Union is fundamentally calling into question projects such as those being developed here behind us," he said. "And that is precisely what we want to prevent."

UPM has invested €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion) in Leuna to convert wood into basic chemicals.

The AfD is sceptical of the European Union, but did not explicitly call for withdrawal from the EU in its 2025 Bundestag election manifesto.

Merz has visited the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, which is also holding an election for its regional parliament later in the month, where he was booed and heckled by passers-by in Kühlungsborn on the Baltic coast. A statement in front of the cameras that had originally been planned was cancelled.

articles.title: Missouri House candidate charged in alleged plot to plant cocaine on opponent
articles.summary: A Republican candidate for the Missouri House is facing federal charges after prosecutors say he orchestrated a plot to plant drugs, including cocaine, on his primary opponent in the lead-up to the August election. Thomas Christopher Ross, 37, made his initial appearance Thursday in a Springfield, Mo., courtroom. He is charged with one count…
articles.body:
A Republican candidate for the Missouri House is facing federal charges after prosecutors say he orchestrated a plot to plant drugs, including cocaine, on his primary opponent in the lead-up to the August election.

Thomas Christopher Ross, 37, made his initial appearance Thursday in a Springfield, Mo., courtroom. He is charged with one count of conspiring to distribute a controlled substance.

A detention hearing has been set for Wednesday, according to court records.

Ross is accused of asking a former campaign manager to place a bag of drugs inside the purse or vehicle of his GOP primary opponent, Louise Secker, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri.

The former campaign manager reportedly told officers with the Joplin Police Department that Ross had given him a black nylon glove containing a small plastic bag of white powder and a pink and white capsule, which were later identified as cocaine and Adderall, respectively.

Authorities said Ross asked the former campaign manager in text messages to plant the drug while he was “out of state on vacation.” The case was turned over to the FBI.

“Candidates are expected to conduct their campaigns with integrity, honesty, and respect for their opponents, allowing voters to make informed decisions without fear of misinformation or undue influence,” U.S. Attorney Matthew Price said in a statement, saying Ross had violated public trust.

Ross defeated Secker in the Republican primary for Missouri House District 161, which covers Joplin and the surrounding area, by only 33 votes.

Peter Kinder, the chair of the Missouri Republican Party, has called for Ross to “immediately” withdraw from the upcoming general election.

“Being the Republican nominee for public office carries with it a responsibility to the voters, the community, and the principles our party represents,” Kinder said in a Wednesday statement. “The people of the 161st District deserve a nominee who can devote his full attention to earning their trust and representing their interests in Jefferson City.”

The Hill has reached out to Ross’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: White House rips ‘activist’ Biden judge who upended Trump birthright citizenship order
articles.summary: A Biden-appointed judge blocked President Donald Trump's birthright citizenship executive order, calling it "almost certainly unconstitutional."
articles.body: A Biden-appointed judge temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's latest executive order seeking to limit birthright citizenship, setting up another high-profile legal battle over the scope of the 14th Amendment. In a 35-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction against the Oval Office's Aug. 6 executive order, which was issued a month after the Supreme Court affirmed birthright citizenship in its ruling in Barbara v. Trump. The injunction is the first to halt Trump's revised birthright citizenship order since the Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship in June. Boardman previously blocked Trump's original birthright citizenship executive order before the Supreme Court weighed in on the issue. Trump's order sought to limit birthright citizenship for children whose parents are deemed alien enemies, including members of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations, and children whose foreign parents paid a surrogate in the U.S. to give birth, among several other restrictions. The executive order prompted Court Appointed Special Advocates (CASA) to file a lawsuit against the Trump administration. TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP FIGHT COMES ROARING BACK WITH ‘INVADERS’ PLAY AFTER KAVANAUGH ROADMAP "The 2026 Executive Order is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth," Boardman wrote in her ruling. "This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them." The White House rejected Boardman's ruling as the work of an "activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda." "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court," Lauren Bis, White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. In a 5-4 decision on the constitutional question of birthright citizenship, the high court held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the country are "citizens at birth" under the 14th Amendment in Barbara v. Trump. TRUMP’S TOUGHER ROUND-TWO BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP STRATEGY HINGES ON KEY LEGAL DISTINCTION, EXPERTS SAY While the Supreme Court has acknowledged exceptions to birthright citizenship, such as children of foreign diplomats or children born during an enemy's hostile occupation of U.S. soil, Boardman rejected Trump's latest executive order targeting children born to alleged alien enemies. She agreed with the plaintiffs' concerns over the Trump administration's "broad view of who qualifies as an enemy." The plaintiffs alleged that the Trump administration had "sometimes resting its conclusions on false or speculative allegations, or even tenuous markers like tattoos or family affiliations." Boardman pointed to two plaintiffs — Andrea, who fled an area of Mexico where a designated cartel operates and whose child’s father has a relative in the group, and Monica, a Venezuelan woman who fears her family could be wrongly linked to Tren de Aragua. TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK "Children whose parents may "rightly or wrongfully" be deemed by the government to be alien enemies face a credible threat of "being denied or stripped of their birthright citizenship... even though they do not fall within a recognized exception to birthright citizenship," Boardman wrote. However, Abhi Kambli, a former Justice Department official, said Boardman was speculating on how the Trump administration could incorrectly bar someone from citizenship based upon being part of a foreign terrorist organization. "Legally, where that falls short is that it's a facial challenge to the entire executive order," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "So, in legal terms, when something's a facial challenge, you have to demonstrate that it's unlawful in all of its applications, and not just the edge, the borderline cases." "She didn't want to wade into the territory of whether that fits as an exception generally within Trump v. Barbara, but she said that based on how they've interpreted it in the past and in terms of what happened with Tren de Aragua and other organizations, she bought into plaintiff speculation that maybe they'll get it wrong this time, and then that'll affect their kids, and then that's why it should get barred," Kambli continued. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Boardman used the First Circuit's language to find that denying citizenship under the new executive order would cause irreparable harm — one of the requirements for issuing a preliminary injunction. "The loss of birthright citizenship — even if temporary and later restored at the conclusion of litigation has cascading effects’ that will ‘very likely leave permanent scars’ on the child and their family," the ruling stated. Monica celebrated the preliminary injunction. "During my pregnancy, I felt so much anxiety over the fact that my child could be born stateless," Monica, said in a statement. "For now, my child and children like mine are protected and guaranteed U.S. citizenship. But I know this isn’t over. The threat to birthright citizenship is still out there. I’ll keep fighting for permanent protection for my child, and for every child born in this country." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the Supreme Court, and lost again today," Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a statement. "The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution. We are very proud to continue this fight alongside the families who have endured more than a year of fear and uncertainty and still refuse to surrender their children’s constitutional rights."

articles.title: Smithsonian showdown intensifies as Trump administration issues a stark new warning
articles.summary: The Smithsonian Institution faces threats beyond its $1 billion federal funding as Trump administration claims evidence of antidiscrimination violations.
articles.body: The Trump administration says it has uncovered evidence that the Smithsonian Institution violated federal nondiscrimination laws and is threatening to withdraw support from its museums unless it corrects course, according to a letter recently made public by the Department of the Interior. "The administration has recently uncovered evidence that the Smithsonian leadership's institutional culture may have resulted in significant violations of Federal antidiscrimination law, including creating a hostile work environment and engaging in practices that classify individuals and allocate opportunities, funding and other benefits on the basis of race, ethnicity and other protected characteristics," a letter sent jointly to the Smithsonian by the DOI and White House reads. Specific evidence of illegal activity on the part of the Smithsonian was not included in the letter, and the DOI did not provide further information when reached for comment. A recent Fox News Digital investigation found that many leading figures at the Smithsonian, including those involved in hiring, have been strong proponents of diversity, equity and inclusion — something the Trump administration has previously framed as racially discriminatory. TRUMP’S SMITHSONIAN CLASH EXPOSES STRIKING PATTERN AMONG MUSEUM CURATORS Conservative political leaders, led by President Donald Trump, have accused the Smithsonian of allowing progressive ideology to shape its presentation of American history. An executive order signed in 2025 directed officials to remove what it called "improper ideology," from the museum. "The Executive Order signed by the President of the United States clearly states ‘the Secretary of the Interior, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, the Administrator of General Services, and the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy shall identify and utilize any and all available authorities to promote the policy of this order and to restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution," a DOI spokesperson told Fox News Digital. TRUMP TARGETS BIDEN-ERA BILLION-DOLLAR SMITHSONIAN BUDGETS AMID ANTI-'WOKE' PUSH Liberals, meanwhile, have framed conservative criticism of the Smithsonian as a partisan attempt to influence the public presentation of history. Unless the Smithsonian remedies the issues outlined in the DOI’s recent letter, as well as the general bias which conservatives allege exists at the institution, the administration says it will consider pulling support from it. The threats this time around, however, differ from the ongoing fight over the roughly $1 billion a year in federal funding the Smithsonian receives. SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY "Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership by, for example, loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants," the letter reads. While the letter does not provide specific changes that the administration would like to see from the Smithsonian, it does note that an "appropriate response" from the organization "must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology." That wording could be significant as the institution operates independently but is overseen by board members appointed by congressional resolutions that the president must sign into law. By October, there will be four openings on the institution’s board of regents, a fact the administration may leverage to increase its influence over the Smithsonian. DOI requests that representatives from the Smithsonian meet with administration officials "at [their] earliest convenience" to discuss the alleged bias and civil rights violations present at the institution. WATCH: SMITHSONIAN HISTORY MUSEUM DIRECTOR STUMBLES OVER BASIC QUESTIONS ON SEX: ‘I’M NOT SURE’ "The museum does not take sides in America’s political debates. We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions," National Museum of American History’s director Anthea Hartig said at a July congressional hearing. The Smithsonian declined to comment on the letter when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday. Recent reporting has found that the museum’s leadership and many of its curators have backgrounds in liberal advocacy or Democratic politics. In addition to exhibits at the National Museum of American History, which the Trump administration characterized as demonizing America, even the Smithsonian-run National Zoo is inundated with information about DEI and gender equity. articles.title: Former podcaster charged with threatening to kill Trump
articles.summary: A former California podcaster has been arrested on charges he repeatedly threatened to kill the president.
articles.body: A former California podcaster has been arrested on charges he repeatedly threatened to kill the president. Benjamin Azariah Southworth, 40, of Los Angeles, engaged in repeated rants on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok in order “to publicly express his hatred toward President Trump and his supporters, and to publicly engage in and/or encourage the abuse, harassment and intimidation of, and violence against, President Trump,” prosecutors said in an indictment made public today. He is expected to be arraigned Thursday in federal district court in Los Angeles, prosecutors added. In one instance, Southworth posted a video “fictitiously depicting himself teleporting into the White House Oval Office, behind President Trump, and raising a knife up to President Trump’s head as if he was about to stab him,” the court filing said. He also sold threatening merch on his website — stickers that said “Kill Trump,” according to prosecutors. Southworth is the former host of the podcast “Yass, Jesus!” and a Christian reality show called “The Remix.” He is additionally charged with cyberstalking and harassing one of the president’s personal attorneys and his family. The person was not named in the indictment, but FBI Director Kash Patel identified the victim as former Trump impeachment lawyer Jay Sekulow in a post on X. “Deadly threats like this are as vile as they are criminal — those responsible will be met by this FBI and law enforcement,” Patel said in the post. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement about Southworth’s arrest that “We will hold perpetrators of violent threats accountable, and anyone who makes these threats online will not be allowed to hide behind their screens.”

articles.body:
Republican strategist Karl Rove expressed his doubts about Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s chances in his November race.

“So, time is running out. If the president wants to have Paxton win, he needs to be tossing a lot of money Paxton’s way so that ads can be run that depict Talarico as the far-left winger that he is,” Rove said on Fox News Radio’s “The Brian Kilmeade Show” on Wednesday.

“If not, Talarico is going to run the message of, ‘My opponent is the most corrupt politician in Texas history,’ all the way to the victory lane,” he added.

In a recent poll , James Talarico (D) was leading Paxton in the Texas Senate race, with 47 percent of respondents saying they would back the Democrat if the election occurred that day, while 40 percent went for the Republican.

Democrats have looked to notch electoral wins in Texas in recent years but haven’t had much success, as seen in 2018 when former Rep. Beto O’Rourke’s (D) challenged Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

While Democrats usually have an uphill battle in the Lone Star State, Paxton comes with notable baggage. The Texas attorney general has been dogged by scandal, previously facing impeachment in the Texas House on corruption charges before being acquitted in the Texas Senate.

Talarico is also facing a favorable electoral environment, as the unpopular war in Iran reached six months, President Trump’s approval rating has slumped and Americans have expressed concerns about the economy in recent polling.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.4 percent on Thursday evening, while his disapproval rating was 57 percent.

articles.title: Postal Service asks Supreme Court to allow Trump’s mail voting changes
articles.summary: The Justice Department urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to clear the way for the U.S. Postal Service to implement President Trump’s executive order targeting mail voting in time for the midterms. The high court previously lifted the judge’s block on the president’s executive order itself. Now, the judge has blocked the Postal Service’s final…
articles.body:
The Justice Department urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to clear the way for the U.S. Postal Service to implement President Trump’s executive order targeting mail voting in time for the midterms.

The high court previously lifted the judge’s block on the president’s executive order itself. Now, the judge has blocked the Postal Service’s final plan .

“The district court’s continued prejudgment of the rule is baseless,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the government’s application.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama who serves on the federal bench in Boston, has so far only temporarily put the Postal Service rule on hold until the next stage of the case.

But with only about 60 days until the midterm elections, the clock is ticking . Sauer noted that North Carolina intends to begin mailing ballots Friday, and Alabama will do so next week.

The Postal Service’s plan would mandate that states’ mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail.

If a ballot doesn’t meet the specifications or someone isn’t on the submitted list, the Postal Service will refuse to deliver it.

The plan has come under legal challenges by blue states and private groups. They argue the rule interferes with state election administration and that the Postal Service has no authority for its plan.

The blue states and private groups suing have until Tuesday morning to respond.

“Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalize the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots,” Sauer wrote to the Supreme Court.

Last month, the high court rebuked the judge by ruling that the states likely have no standing to sue over Trump’s executive order itself. Talwani’s new order focuses on the Postal Service’s plan to implement the president’s directive, which was only finalized in recent days.

She held a hearing earlier Thursday on whether to block the Postal Service’s plan indefinitely but has yet to rule.

articles.body:
Vice President Vance on Thursday quipped he was “really looking forward” to seeing former President Biden at a New York City memorial service marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

“As you can probably guess, I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden,” Vance said during a press briefing.

“I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and you know, it’ll be great. We’ll have a great time with Joe Biden and the other presidents,” he added, while laughing.

In addition to Biden, former Presidents Obama, Clinton and George W. Bush are expected to attend the Ground Zero ceremony, according to NewsNation. Former first ladies Jill Biden, Laura Bush and Hillary Clinton are also anticipated to be in attendance, The New York Times reported .

Sept. 11 will mark the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks, which killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and on board a hijacked United Airlines plane that crashed in Pennsylvania.

The vice president was also asked by a reporter about why he and not President Trump was going to the New York ceremony.

The question followed reporting from The New York Times last week that the president decided not to attend the memorial service, partly because the event’s organizers denied his request to give a speech. The ceremony has barred political speeches since 2012.

Trump strongly refuted the reporting, calling it “more Corrupt News” in a Truth Social post.

“I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a ‘solemn ceremony!’” he wrote, adding that he would “love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time.”

The president is expected to attend a memorial service at the Pentagon on this year’s anniversary, while Vance will represent the White House at the New York event.

Vance said the decision about who attended which event was “decided as a team.”

“I will say, as much as it’s tragic — and it was a terrible day — I am looking forward to it because it’s such an amazing honor to be able to get to go to New York and to share in that moment where the parents and the kids read the names of the people who lost their lives,” he added.

The latest push comes as the data center build-out has increasingly become politically “toxic,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and head of the advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI.

“The AI industry is losing and has been [losing] on this issue pretty much all year,” he told The Hill, adding, “The American people are skeptical of AI, skeptical of Big Tech, and the companies are trying to reverse that trend, and it’s going to be very difficult.”

Trump finds himself “ caught between this massive movement by his base that is skeptical of data centers and AI and the moneyed interests in Big Tech that are funding a lot of candidates and funding the party and even White House projects,” Steinhauser said.

articles.title: Jim Justice considering run for West Virginia governor
articles.summary: West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice (R) said Thursday he is considering a run at the governor’s mansion in 2028, after leaving it to join the upper chamber less than two years ago. During an appearance on MetroNews’s “Talkline” radio show, Justice said he was “100 percent” considering a primary challenge to incumbent West Virginia Gov.…
articles.body:
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice (R) said Thursday he is considering a run at the governor’s mansion in 2028, after leaving it to join the upper chamber less than two years ago.

During an appearance on MetroNews’s “Talkline” radio show, Justice said he was “100 percent” considering a primary challenge to incumbent West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey (R) — who succeeded the first-term senator last year.

“I’m not going to tease around with people, that’s awful to do,” Justice added. “That’s not my style. We’ll make a decision and make it quickly.”

Politico first reported Thursday on Justice’s consideration of a primary challenge to Morrisey.

The 75-year-old West Virginia senator served two terms as governor from 2017 to 2025. The Republican convert defeated Democrat Glenn Elliott by more than 40 points to secure his Senate seat in 2024, eight years after Justice won his first governor’s race as a Democrat.

Justice announced he was switching parties at a rally alongside President Trump, after he did not publicly back 2016 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton.

If Justice, a businessman worth hundreds of millions, were to seek a third term as governor, it would pit him against his successor in Morrisey.

Justice did not back Morrisey in the 2024 GOP gubernatorial primary, instead endorsing Moore Capito — now the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of West Virginia and the son of West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R).

Morrisey said Thursday that Justice running for governor is the “last thing I want to focus on,” noting he is roughly 20 months into his first term.

“I want to deliver. I want to keep delivering on big wins for West Virginia, like we announced today. Helping our families, not playing politics,” he told reporters. “I want to make sure that we’re doing those really incredible things to help families who are struggling, that’s what my focus is.”

The former and incumbent West Virginia governors exchanged verbal blows last week, when Morrisey praised a deal under which Justice sold his controlling interest in West Virginia’s Greenbrier resort.

“I am hopeful that the new controlling owner will bring much needed financial stability to the iconic Greenbrier resort,” Morrisey wrote on social platform X .

Justice fired back, saying his successor as governor “seems awfully eager to take shots at people who actually take risks, build businesses and create jobs” in West Virginia.

“I’ve spent my life doing exactly that — signing the front of paychecks for thousands of West Virginians, not just collecting one,” the senator wrote on X .

He later added, “Patrick can keep playing politics. We’ll keep building.”

That prompted a response from Morrisey. Replying to Justice on X, the governor wrote , “I wish you the best, but you can’t blame me or anyone else for your financial mismanagement in losing The Greenbrier.”

Morrisey continued, “I hope you’ll join the Greenbrier’s new leadership and me in keeping jobs in West Virginia while restoring the resort to its former glory. Keep the faith!”

During his “Talkline” interview Thursday, Justice said he hopes Morrisey and state officials “knock it out of the park.” But the senator noted he will make a decision about challenging his successor next year “real soon.”

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial jurors excused again after defense blames one for deadlock
articles.summary: The jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial was sent home again Thursday afternoon after her defense attorney blamed one “spurned” juror for causing deliberations to extend into Friday, which would be their seventh consecutive day. Jurors appear to be split 11-1 and will return to court Friday morning for another day of discussions, seeking to…
articles.body:
The jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial was sent home again Thursday afternoon after her defense attorney blamed one “spurned” juror for causing deliberations to extend into Friday, which would be their seventh consecutive day.

Jurors appear to be split 11-1 and will return to court Friday morning for another day of discussions, seeking to reach a verdict on whether or not Clancy is criminally liable for the murders of her three children.

In a tense exchange on Thursday, before the jury was sent home, Clancy’s defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan to eject one juror who he claimed “refuses to listen to the law.” Sullivan had earlier in the day spoken to jurors about the legal definition of “reasonable doubt.”

“If we come back here in a half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, it’s a shame. It’s a real shame,” Reddington said.

Clancy is facing three counts of first-degree murder for the fatal strangulations of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan in the basement of her Duxbury, Mass., home.

Clancy’s attorneys say she was struggling with postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids, rendering her not criminally responsible for her actions. Prosecutors argue Clancy willfully planned these killings while her husband was out of the house.

The judge has repeatedly urged the jury to keep trying to reach a unanimous decision to avoid a mistrial. The jury — which consists of nine women and three men — can convict Clancy of first-degree murder, rule in favor of a reduced charge such as manslaughter or find her not guilty due to insanity.

Sullivan spoke to the jurors collectively on Thursday about the legal definition of reasonable doubt after swearing each in one by one. They were then sent back to continue their deliberations before the judge later excused them for the day.

The prosecution told Sullivan they had no objection to the jury’s questions or the judge’s redirection.

Sullivan said he did not “feel that it was proper” for him to comply with Reddington’s request to remove this jury member, noting this was a “sensitive undertaking.”

“I don’t feel it’s appropriate for me to say I agree with one juror or the 11,” the judge said. “At this point, I’ve asked if they are able to follow my instructions … They swore earlier that they could. They’ve said at this point that they can.”

If acquitted, Clancy would be sent to a state psychiatric hospital instead of facing jail time, where she would be reviewed periodically to determine if she can safely live in a community, The Boston Globe reported .

articles.title: Missouri Supreme Court rules new GOP-drawn map can’t be used for November elections
articles.summary: The court said a referendum seeking to put the map up for a vote must be placed on the ballot, meaning the state’s elections this fall will take place under its old congressional lines.
articles.body: The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a blow to Republicans. The court ruled that a referendum on whether the state can use the map going forward must be included on the November ballot, meaning Missouri’s fall elections will take place under its previous district lines. The new map was designed to draw one of the two Missouri Democrats in Congress, longtime Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, out of his seat. “More than 305,000 Missourians demanded a say in who will represent them in the halls of Congress. Despite the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence many of our neighbors, the people fought back and won,” Cleaver said in a post on X following the ruling, adding that “democracy prevails.” The ruling comes after a protracted battle between advocacy group People Not Politicians Missouri, which sought to block the Republican redistricting effort, and the state GOP leaders who defended it. Missouri redrew its congressional map in 2025 at the behest of President Donald Trump. In response, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a veto referendum. And while the group exceeded the signature requirements for getting on the ballot, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify it, saying that it was unconstitutional. The group appealed to the state Supreme Court, which heard arguments on the matter on Wednesday. The ruling comes just days before the state’s Sept. 8 deadline to finalize its ballot for the general election. The state ran its August primary election using the Republican-drawn map. Judge Ginger K. Gooch wrote in her ruling that Hoskins and those acting with him “are restrained and enjoined from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in HB 1 for the November 2026 general election or at any other time thereafter unless and until HB 1 is approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election and takes effect 30 days thereafter.” The court’s decision means Cleaver will now be seeking re-election for his old seat, which skews heavily Democratic. He won by almost 24 percentage points in 2024. The redesigned 5th District, which was struck down by Thursday’s ruling, was drawn so that Trump would have won by more than 17 points in 2024. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway vowed in a statement following the ruling to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court. “Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway wrote. “We are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised—which is what today’s decision does.” People Not Politicians executive director Richard von Glahn celebrated the ruling. “This victory reaches beyond Missouri. In a year when map-drawing has become a national weapon, courts across the country are watching what happens here. A Missouri win for the referendum is a signal that the people still hold the power,” von Glahn said in a statement. Missouri is one of a handful of Republican-led states that took up mid-decade redistricting efforts at Trump’s urging to shore up the party’s narrow House majority. Trump criticized the ruling in a Truth Social post, calling the ruling “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional.” “The Election Process, as usual, is being disturbed in America! Missouri must be able to use the map that was in effect just a couple of months ago, in the Primary,” Trump wrote. The last time one of the state’s maps was considered by a voter referendum was in 1922, after the Republican-led state Legislature redrew the districts. Voters at the time rejected the new map.

articles.title: Missouri Supreme Court throws out GOP-favored House maps
articles.summary: The Missouri Supreme Court dealt a blow to President Trump and Republicans Thursday, ruling the GOP could not issue a new map aimed at giving the party an additional seat in the House until the congressional lines are approved by voters in November. The decision is a setback for Republicans, who had sought to quickly…
articles.body:
The Missouri Supreme Court dealt a blow to President Trump and Republicans Thursday, ruling the GOP could not issue a new map aimed at giving the party an additional seat in the House until the congressional lines are approved by voters in November.

The decision is a setback for Republicans, who had sought to quickly pass a new GOP-friendly 7-1 map in the House this cycle, meant to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) district and give the Republican Party one more pickup opportunity.

Instead, the high court ruled that a citizen-led referendum aiming to halt the implementation of the map and put it to a vote in November could proceed.

The congressional lines “did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters,” the court said in its decision. “The congressional redistricting the General Assembly established in 2022 remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.”

Missouri Democrats swiftly declared victory.

“The Missouri Supreme Court just unanimously ruled to reverse the gerrymandered, anti-democracy maps until THE PEOPLE have a chance to vote. This is only possible because of the work done by our neighbors to gather signatures and fight back!” the party said on the social platform X.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (R) said her office would “immediately” seek relief from the Supreme Court.

“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway said in a post on X.

Missouri Republicans last year moved forward with redistricting amid pressure from the White House and national Republicans to join a redistricting tit-for-tat with blue states that had kicked off in red Texas.

Republicans already hold six of eight House seats, but the new map would have dismantled Cleaver’s Kansas City district to make the seat more winnable for the GOP.

Missouri’s Supreme Court previously ruled this spring that state lawmakers did not violate the state constitution in redrawing the maps. A Cole County judge also rejected an effort to suspend the new maps as organizers gathered signatures to challenge them.

In early August, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) blocked the referendum, declaring the petition led by People Not Politicians unconstitutional and triggering a lawsuit after the group had turned in more than 300,000 signatures to get it on the ballot. Hoskins argued that, under the state constitution, redistricting plans approved by the General Assembly aren’t subject to a referendum process.

But the seven-member Missouri Supreme Court — on which five of its judges were appointed by a Republican governor — unanimously ruled that the referendum petition was “legal, sufficient, and timely” and that Hoskins “incorrectly concluded otherwise.”

Barring intervention from the nation’s highest court, voters are now set to have the final say in November on whether the maps take effect in 2028.

For the time being, the court said Missouri’s congressional districts established in 2022 “remain in full force and effect for this year’s general election.”

articles.summary: The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony and killed four people on Tuesday.

The US military is investigating Iranian claims that its strikes killed at least four people including two children at a wedding in southern Iran, Vice-President JD Vance has said.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) - a humanitarian group - said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony at a home in Sirik on Tuesday, prompting Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei to declare it a "war crime".

US missiles were fired the same day over "attempted attacks" by Iran on American forces, but a US Central Command spokesperson said it "never targets civilians".

Speaking on Thursday, Vance said he was "extremely sceptical" over reports of the alleged strike but confirmed the US would investigate.

Iran says US strike killed four at wedding in 'war crime' as US denies targeting civilians

"I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far. So I'm extremely sceptical of this," Vance told a White House briefing.

Iran has launched fresh attacks on US bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates in response to the alleged strike.

The IRCS said 67 people were hurt when shrapnel from the missile hit a family wedding ceremony, killing at least four people. Iranian state media said a fifth person, a woman aged 22, had died in hospital shortly after.

The four people killed were named locally as Zarkhatoon Taheri, 50; Kolsum Mallahi Nazhdnia, 43; Mohammad Mallahi, 16; and Amirali Karimi, four.

BBC Verify confirmed a video and two images taken on Tuesday near Kuhestak's coast that showed a telecommunications tower being destroyed, and other videos from Tuesday and Wednesday showed severely damaged houses about 130m (427ft) north of the tower.

BBC Persian Forensics found the telecommunications tower was about 112m (367 ft) from the house where the wedding was being held.

articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Judge halts EPA effort to overturn California car rules A federal judge late Wednesday temporarily blocked a Trump administration effort to overturn California’s clean car rules through Congress. J. David Ake, Getty Images Judge Beryl Howell, an appointee of former President Obama, blocked an Environmental Protection…
articles.body:
Judge halts EPA effort to overturn California car rules

A federal judge late Wednesday temporarily blocked a Trump administration effort to overturn California’s clean car rules through Congress.

Judge Beryl Howell, an appointee of former President Obama, blocked an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) move that would have allowed Congress and President Trump to overturn California rules related to vehicle and lawn equipment emissions.

In years past, the EPA allowed these regulations to move forward by granting waivers that exempted them from the Clean Air Act’s preemption of state laws that are stricter than federal standards.

In June, the agency classified these waivers as “rules,” an effort to let Congress overturn them using the Congressional Review Act (CRA), which allows lawmaker to nix recently passed rules with simple majority votes and presidential approval.

“The central problem for EPA is that the waivers themselves explicitly state that they are not rules, while the CRA limits invocation of this statute only to agency rules of general applicability, which EPA, in its own words, has emphatically stated Clean Air Act waiver orders are not,” Howell wrote in her ruling.

She said that the agency was trying to get the court to engage in “Orwellian doublethink, offering two explanations simultaneously” for its move.

In her ruling, Howell said that California is likely to ultimately succeed on the merits of the case, and she ordered a return to the status quo prior to the EPA’s June action. In an unsigned statement, the EPA said it is “considering immediate appeal options.”

articles.title: Pentagon sought to divert NIH funds for defense use, top House Appropriations Democrat says
articles.summary: The Pentagon is attempting to divert billions of dollars from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to bolster the agency’s budget, according to the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) in a statement Thursday said Trump administration officials only recently disclosed to Congress that the Defense Department signed an interagency agreement…
articles.body:
The Pentagon is attempting to divert billions of dollars from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to bolster the agency’s budget, according to the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) in a statement Thursday said Trump administration officials only recently disclosed to Congress that the Defense Department signed an interagency agreement that could give the Pentagon access to billions of dollars meant for biomedical research.

“This secretive attempt to siphon research funds away from NIH is outrageous. The interagency agreement needs to be terminated immediately,” DeLauro said in a statement.

“Circumventing Congress to divert money intended to help Americans who are exposed to HIV, influenza, tuberculosis, and other deadly diseases—and directing those funds to the Department of Defense—is beyond the pale,” DeLauro added.

The Democrat said the agreement would pull from the NIH’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), its leading institute for infectious-disease research.

DeLauro did not say the NIH signed the agreement.

The NIH and the Pentagon “explored potential avenues of collaboration to support the development of medical technologies, such as therapeutics, diagnostics, and personal protective equipment (PPE), to protect against infectious diseases [and] other health risks that Americans face,” a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement to The Hill.

A partnership between the NIH and the Pentagon “would enable nimble multi-agency resources to collaboratively respond to public health emergencies, such as the recent Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson added.

It wasn’t clear how much money the Pentagon was seeking or what it would be used to fund. The Pentagon did not immediately return a request for comment.

According to Sen. Patty Murray (Wash.), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, the agreement establishes a framework for the Pentagon to “potentially tap billions of dollars in funding.”

Both Murray and DeLauro said the agreement was not proactively shared with Congress. According to DeLauro, it was only disclosed after House Democrats pressed NIH officials.

DeLauro accused the Pentagon of attempting to make up for shortfalls caused by the war in Iran. The agency is awaiting congressional approval of a $95 billion supplemental funding request that would mainly go toward the war.

“It is no secret that the Department of Defense is facing enormous financial pressure because of President Trump’s war of choice with Iran. But the Trump administration cannot make American patients, families, and scientists pay the price,” DeLauro said.

Patient advocates were quick to condemn the potential arrangement. “Congressionally-appropriated funding for NIH research to save lives and improve the health of Americans should not be treated like a slush fund,” Erika Sward, executive director of United for Cures, said in a statement. “We call on Congress to investigate this and ensure money appropriated for lifesaving research is used as intended.”
