articles.body:
What to know about respiratory vaccine recommendations

Several medical groups have joined together to release 2026-2027 respiratory virus immunization recommendations , filling a void left by the relative silence from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The groups include the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

The recommendations were informed by a joint review of the evidence for flu , COVID and RSV vaccines conducted by the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project. That review was published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA.

Such a review is typically conducted by a CDC advisory panel, in conjunction with medical groups. But the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices has been dismantled under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy fired all members of the panel last year and replaced them with largely with vaccine skeptics.

A lawsuit against that restructuring has temporarily left the panel, and its recommendations, in legal limbo . The CDC on Tuesday updated its clinical guidance for the flu vaccine to follow last year’s recommendations, but it did not mention the new mRNA shots available for older adults that FDA recently approved.

All children 6 months and older receive the flu vaccine;

All children ages 6-23 months receive the COVID-19 vaccine, while children 2-18 years old get the shot if they’re in certain risk groups or simply want it;

All children 8 months and younger get the RSV shot if their mother did not get vaccinated while pregnant, while children ages 8-19 months in their second RSV season get the shot if they’re in certain risk groups for severe disease.

For adults, the groups generally recommend everyone get the annual COVID-19 and flu shots, while adults 50-74 years of age get the RSV shot once if they have an increased risk of developing severe RSV.

RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall .

articles.body:
President Trump announced Thursday evening that Adam Telle, the current assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, will be the acting Army secretary following this week’s resignation of Dan Driscoll.

“He is a Great Patriot, who is respected by all,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post announcing Telle’s appointment.

As assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, Telle oversaw public works functions and civil engineering, carrying out the Trump administration’s priorities when it comes to waterways, ports and flood control infrastructure overseen by the Army Corps of Engineers.

Telle is assuming the acting Army secretary role “effective immediately,” Trump said.

Trump’s announcement comes a day after Driscoll, a close ally of Vice President Vance, left the position after months of internal clashes with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Driscoll’s departure highlighted Hegseth’s ambition to impose his will on the Army. The Pentagon chief has recently removed a number of its senior military officers — including Gen. Randy George, the Army’s chief of staff, along with Gen. Chris Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa.

Driscoll broke silence about his departure late Tuesday, saying his last full day as secretary would be on Wednesday. He did not share the reason for his departure.

“As a third-generation Army veteran, it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve as the Secretary of the Army under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. Tomorrow is my last full day in the role,” Driscoll said in a statement. “Our Soldiers, Civilians and their Families are our Nation’s very best and they have inspired me every day. I am sincerely thankful for their service and sacrifice.”

Telle has spent his career on Capitol Hill working for Senate Republicans.

Before being nominated for the assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works post, Telle worked as Sen. Bill Hagerty’s (R-Tenn.) chief of staff.

The acting Army secretary appointee also worked in the White House Office of Legislative Affairs during Trump’s first term. He was confirmed by the Senate for his Civil Works position last year in a 72-22 vote.

“Huge congrats to Adam. Strong and whip smart,” Hegseth wrote on social media Thursday. “He is indeed a great Patriot — and will be an immediate asset to the @USArmy.”

articles.title: Maryland’s top court allows Democratic-backed congressional redistricting measure on November ballot
articles.summary: Maryland voters will get to decide in November on a congressional redistricting amendment being pushed by Democrats as part of a nationwide battle for control of the U.S.
articles.body: Maryland voters will get to decide in November on a congressional redistricting amendment being pushed by Democrats as part of a nationwide battle for control of the U.S. House in future elections. The Maryland Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the proposed constitutional amendment must be placed on the November ballot, reversing two lower court rulings that had blocked it from going to voters. But the court directed the ballot summary to be rewritten. The decision marks a notable victory for Democrats, who are trying to counter a Republican redistricting movement pushed by President Donald Trump. Democrats already hold seven of Maryland’s eight U.S. House seats. The proposed amendment would not change voting districts for the midterm elections. But if approved by voters, it could free Democratic lawmakers to draw new congressional districts that give the party a shot at a clean sweep in the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore called lawmakers into a special session in August to refer the amendment to the November ballot. The amendment would undo the foundation of a 2022 court ruling that struck down a previous Democratic redistricting plan as a “product of extreme partisan gerrymandering.” That judge said a constitutional provision requiring compact districts that respect “natural boundaries” applied to congressional districts. But the proposed amendment would apply those parameters only to state legislative districts. That could allow lawmakers to draw congressional districts that cross the Chesapeake Bay, potentially reshaping a district held by U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s only Republican representative and the chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus. Lower courts ruled that lawmakers didn’t abide by their own requirements when referring the amendment to the ballot. At the heart of the case was a law passed earlier this year that set a July 1 deadline for the secretary of state to certify information about statewide ballot questions to the Maryland State Board of Elections. The same law also set a 15-day public comment period. Those deadlines had already passed by the time lawmakers approved the redistricting amendment on Aug. 4. Lawyers for Democratic Attorney General Anthony Brown argued that those deadlines didn’t matter. They said that law didn’t apply to the redistricting amendment because lawmakers wrote their own ballot summary for it, using their constitutional authority. The state Supreme Court ultimately agreed. Republican lawmakers who sued had won in lower courts on claims that the ballot question wording was misleading and that the amendment violated a single-issue requirement in the state constitution by including a provision giving original jurisdiction over congressional redistricting lawsuits to the state Supreme Court. The state Supreme Court rejected the multiple-subject argument but concurred that the ballot wording was misleading. However, the court said that wasn’t enough to prevent the amendment from going to the people. It instead directed a change to be made to the ballot wording that voters will see. Redistricting typically happens near the beginning of each decade, after new census data is released. But a mid-decade redistricting battle broke out last year after Trump urged Republican-led states to redraw congressional districts in the hopes that it might help Republicans hold on to a slim House majority in this year’s midterm elections. Republicans hope to win as many as 16 additional seats this year from new U.S. House districts enacted in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas. Democrats hope to gain as many as five congressional seats from new districts in California and Utah. In May, the Virginia Supreme Court struck down a redistricting effort that could have helped Democrats win up to four additional seats. It ruled that the Democratic-led legislature violated procedural requirements when placing an amendment on the ballot.

articles.title: Trump administration warns agencies could stop helping Smithsonian
articles.summary: The Trump administration is threatening to cut off federal agencies’ participation with the Smithsonian Institution, accusing its leaders of promoting a “culture of ideological activism” — the latest move in an ongoing dispute surrounding the world’s largest museum complex’s presentation of exhibits about the U.S. In a letter to Smithsonian leaders last Friday, Interior Secretary…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is threatening to cut off federal agencies’ participation with the Smithsonian Institution, accusing its leaders of promoting a “culture of ideological activism” — the latest move in an ongoing dispute surrounding the world’s largest museum complex’s presentation of exhibits about the U.S.

In a letter to Smithsonian leaders last Friday, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the president’s assistant for domestic policy, Vince Haley, cited a July White House report , which they said identified “alarming examples” of “radical ideology” across museum exhibits and programming.

“In addition to the more than $1 billion appropriated to the Smithsonian by Congress each year, the Smithsonian enjoys support from executive departments and agencies,” the officials wrote in their letter.

“Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership by, for example, loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants,” they continued.

The two administration officials requested the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents meet with them to discuss the findings of the White House report.

The Smithsonian Institute declined to comment.

In July, the president directed the National Park Service to install disclaimers outside of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History (NMAH) stating some of the museum’s exhibits contain “inaccurate information” about the nation’s past.

The executive order , titled “Restoring trust in the Smithsonian Institution,” also cited the White House report on the museum complex’s exhibits to justify the new, temporary signage.

“The Report demonstrates that the Smithsonian leadership does not present American history as a shared national inheritance to be taught and celebrated, but instead views American history as a ‘prime tool’ to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society,” the president said in the order.

Trump directed his administration to “take all available steps” to address the issues identified by this report.

NMAH Director Anthea Hartig defended the museum against Republican criticism during testimony before a congressional panel in July, telling lawmakers the White House report “does not fairly or accurately” capture the museum’s exhibits.

“The museum does not take sides in America’s political debates,” Hartig said. “We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions.”

articles.title: GOP candidate gets busted trying to plant drugs on his political rival
articles.summary: Thomas Ross allegedly conspired to plant cocaine and Adderall in his Republican rival's purse, but his campaign manager wore a wire for the FBI.
articles.body: A Republican candidate for the Missouri state House is facing federal drug charges after newly unsealed court documents revealed an alleged plot to frame his political opponent by planting cocaine and prescription pills in her purse. Thomas Christopher Ross, 37, made his initial court appearance Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri in Springfield, where he faced one count of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance. According to the Justice Department (DOJ), Ross allegedly conspired with his former campaign manager to stash narcotics among the personal property of his Republican rival, Louise Secker, ahead of the state's August primary. But, according to the unsealed FBI affidavit, the campaign manager reportedly flipped on Ross and ultimately wore a wire to catch him in a sting operation. VULNERABLE DEM'S OWN AUDIT ADMITS MEDICAID OVERSIGHT FAILURE AMID MASSIVE STATEWIDE FRAUD SCANDAL "The circumstances of his arrest are serious and deeply troubling," said Peter Kinder, chairman of the Missouri Republican Party, after news of Ross's arrest. "Being the Republican nominee for public office carries with it a responsibility to the voters, the community and the principles our party represents ... given the seriousness of the situation, I believe the right course of action is clear." Kinder called on Ross to drop out of the race, as he just narrowly won the Republican nomination for Missouri's state House of Representatives District 161 earlier this month by just a handful of votes against Secker to advance to the November general election against Democrat Aaaron Metzger. Under Missouri election law, Ross has until Sept. 8 to voluntarily withdraw his name from the November general election ballot. DON'T LET FAKE ELECTION WEBSITES FOOL YOU BEFORE 2026 MIDTERMS "The American people deserve confidence in an electoral process that has served our nation for generations," Matthew Price, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Missouri, said in a Justice Department press release published Thursday. "Candidates are expected to conduct their campaigns with integrity, honesty, and respect for their opponents, allowing voters to make informed decisions without fear of misinformation or undue influence." The DOJ said it was contacted on July 30 by the Joplin Police Department (JPD) regarding claims of public corruption, after Ross's campaign manager told JPD about the conspiracy to plant cocaine and an Adderall pill – both Schedule II narcotics – among Secker's belongings. The staffer said he was asked by Ross to plant the baggie of cocaine and prescription amphetamine pill, both given to him by Ross, inside Secker's purse, or car. The Justice Department added that the drugs were meant to be planted while Ross was out of town. MAN ACCUSED OF USING FAKE CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS SIGNATURE TO GET OWN CRIMINAL CASE DISMISSED According to a probable cause affidavit, the following day, on July 31, the campaign staffer wore a wire during an encounter at Ross's home, reported KOLR-TV. The outlet said the court records showed how the campaign manager told Ross he still had "the bag and addies" and asked if Ross still wanted the drugs planted on his opponent. Ross reportedly responded in the affirmative, per the court documents, and the pair also sent numerous text messages discussing the conspiracy that Ross suggested "would be extreme egg on the face" for Secker. Screenshots of text messages suggest Ross and the former campaign manager discussed the plot as early as May 31, local outlet KCUR-FM out of Kansas City added. articles.title: Excavation set to begin on Trump administration's 250-foot triumphal arch amid legal battle
articles.summary: Doug Burgum announced excavation on the 250-foot Great Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C., but a lawsuit challenges the project's authorization.
articles.body: Excavation work will begin over the next two weeks on a site where the Trump administration plans to build a tall memorial arch in Washington, D.C., a project that currently faces a lawsuit from opponents who argue the project will disrupt nearby historic sight lines. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum on Thursday announced that work would start on the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck, which will be located on Columbia Island, standing between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. "This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World," Burgum wrote on X, along with mock-ups of the towering 250-foot-tall arch. LEAVITT SHOWS OFF US TRIUMPHAL ARCH, WITH PLANS TO BE RELEASED THURSDAY The images showed a white arch with gold detail, with "ONE NATION UNDER GOD" written on top. A gold Lady Liberty-like figure with wings and a torch stands above, as well as gold eagles with their wings spread outward. The project faces opposition from three veterans and an architectural historian who argued that "congressional authorization is necessary and lacking for this project," said Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group representing the plaintiffs. WHITE HOUSE TOUTS TRUMP’S ‘BOLD VISION’ FOR TOWERING INDEPENDENCE ARCH FOR AMERICA 250 "We believe that construction cannot and should not proceed apace, and we are prepared to inform the court that it needs to, at this juncture, step in," Sansone told The Associated Press. A 24-page report released last month by the National Park Service backs the idea for the arch. However, the report noted that the project would have "direct and indirect adverse effects on the sight lines of historic properties." TRUMP'S PLAN FOR TRIUMPHAL ARCH MOVES STEP CLOSER TO REALITY In a series of posts on X, Burgum defended the project, saying the idea for a monument goes back decades. He cited attempts by past Congresses and old reports about discussions of the construction of a memorial. The secretary noted that more than 70 cities, including Athens, London, Madrid, New Delhi, Paris and Rome, showcase arches. "Interestingly, Washington, DC, is the only major Western capital without an arch," he wrote. "Now after 125 years of waiting, the most powerful capital in the world will be the home of the most spectacular and beautiful arch of them all!" TRUMP’S DC BEAUTIFICATION PUSH WINS RARE DEM PRAISE AS PRESIDENT SNAPS LANDMARKS BACK TO LIFE Fox News Digital has reached out to the Interior Department and the Public Citizen Litigation Group. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The arch is one of several projects undertaken by the Trump administration, including the renaming of the Kennedy Center, a new White House ballroom and the refurbishing of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
